title: Four ways to get server-initiated data to a client

spec.title: Four ways to get server-initiated data to a client
spec.description: HTTP is request/response: the client asks, the server answers. Anything that needs the server to speak first has to work around that, and the four workarounds trade latency against compatibility.

steps.text: Polling asks repeatedly. Trivial to build, and you pay a full request cycle for an overwhelmingly empty answer — 10,000 clients polling every 3 seconds is 3,300 requests per second to mostly say 'no'. Latency is also bounded below by the interval.

Long polling holds the request open until there is something to send. Latency drops to near zero and idle traffic nearly vanishes. It works through every proxy and firewall, which is its main virtue — but each message costs a reconnect.

Server-Sent Events keep one HTTP response open and stream into it, with automatic browser reconnection. Efficient and simple — but one-directional, so a chat client would pair it with ordinary POSTs. Ideal for notification feeds, where traffic really is server-to-client only.

WebSocket upgrades the connection and both sides send frames over one persistent TCP connection. Lowest latency and lowest per-message overhead — the standard answer for chat, with long polling kept as a fallback where WebSocket is blocked.

A million concurrent users means a million open sockets whether or not anyone is typing — file descriptors and kernel buffers, on the order of tens of kilobytes each. It also makes servers stateful: a user's connection lives on one specific machine, so delivering to them needs a registry mapping user to server plus an internal hop.

None of that applies to polling or SSE behind a CDN. So the choice is not 'WebSocket is best' — it is how much operational surface the feature justifies. If updates are infrequent and one-directional, the simpler option avoids an entire class of problem.
